questions.question: Define market failure and discuss its causes as listed in the syllabus.
questions.expected_answer: Market failure exists when the price mechanism allocates resources inefficiently — the quantities produced and consumed differ from the socially optimal quantities, so a different allocation could raise society's welfare. Six causes: (1) externalities — costs or benefits landing on third parties outside the transaction, ignored by the price; (2) missing markets — public goods, being non-rivalrous and non-excludable, cannot be charged for (free-rider problem) so their markets never form, while merit goods are under-supplied and demerit goods over-consumed; (3) imperfect competition — monopolies and cartels price above marginal cost and restrict output below the social optimum; (4) imperfect information — buyers, workers or lenders acting on wrong or incomplete knowledge choose wrong quantities; (5) immobility of factors — labour and capital that cannot move to their best use, as with structural unemployment in declining mining towns; (6) inequality of income distribution — markets weight demand by purchasing power, so resources follow the rand votes of the rich toward luxuries while urgent needs backed by no money go unmet.

questions.question: Using the concepts of private and social costs and benefits, explain with described diagrams why a polluting factory over-produces and vaccination is under-produced, and outline the state's corrective toolkit.
questions.expected_answer: Social cost is private cost plus external cost; social benefit is private benefit plus external benefit. For the polluting mill: quantity on the horizontal axis, price on the vertical; demand slopes down, the mill's marginal private cost (supply) slopes up, and the marginal social cost curve runs parallel above it, the gap being the external cost per ton. The market settles where demand crosses private cost — large output, low price; society's optimum is where demand crosses social cost — smaller output, higher price. Goods with external costs are thus over-produced and under-priced. For vaccination the mirror holds: the social benefit curve runs above private demand, so the social optimum quantity (where social benefit crosses supply) exceeds the market quantity — external-benefit goods are under-produced. The toolkit: taxes equal to external costs (carbon tax, fuel levy, sin taxes, sugary drinks levy) lift private cost onto social cost; subsidies on external benefits (no-fee schools, free primary healthcare); direct state provision of public goods; regulation such as emission standards and information rules; maximum and minimum prices (with shortage and surplus side effects); and redistribution. Each instrument carries costs — wrong levels, financing, distortions and public sector failure — so each needs case-by-case justification.

questions.question: Explain the steps of cost-benefit analysis, why it is the appropriate tool for public projects, and evaluate its limitations.
questions.expected_answer: CBA compares all social costs with all social benefits of a project, private and external alike. Steps: identify every cost (construction, operation, flooded farmland, relocated households, lost wetlands); identify every benefit (electricity, flood prevention, jobs, time saved, health gains); attach money values including to unpriced items (time at the wage rate, a wetland at the cost of the treatment plant doing the same job, risk to life via willingness to pay); discount future values to the present, since a rand in twenty years is worth less than one today; and compare, proceeding if social benefits exceed social costs or ranking competing projects by benefit-cost ratio. It suits public projects because it internalises on paper what markets ignore — externalities, unpriced goods, third parties — where private profit measures only the private slice. Limitations: valuing the unpriceable is contestable; the discount rate is a moral choice disguised as arithmetic — a high rate silences future generations, which is why climate projects hinge on it; project champions overstate benefits and understate costs (optimism bias); and CBA sums rands without asking whose, so a passing project can still burden the poorest — distribution and compensation of losers must be judged alongside the total.
